## Background

Today we explore some unsupervised machine learning techniques that are very popular in bioinformatics, including clustering and dimentionality reduction methods.

## K-means clustering

The main funciotn in "base R" for K-means is called `kmeans()`.

Before going deep lets's make up some data to cluster where we know what the answer should be. For this we can use the `rnorm()`.

```{r}
rnorm(10)
```

```{r}
hist(rnorm(10000))
```

#### Q. Return 30 numbers centered at +3 and another 30 centered at -3.

```{r}
x <- c( rnorm(30, mean=3),
        rnorm(30, mean=-3) )
x
```

```{r}
z <- cbind(x=x, y=rev(x))
head(z)
```

```{r}
plot(z)
```

Reminder on how to find out what you need for a new function:
```{r}
?kmeans()
```

Now let's use it
```{r}
k <- kmeans(z, centers=2)
k
```
> This list of "available componants" are saved in a list that you can access via `k$[wvr componant you want]`

#### Q. How do you get at the main clustering result (i.e. the "clustering vector")
```{r}
k$cluster
```

#### Q. Make a results figure showing our data colored by cluster membership. Bonus: add cluster centers in a different color.

```{r}
plot(z, col=k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col=4, pch=16, cex=1.5)
```

#### Run `kmeans()` again and cluster into 4 groups and show the results in a figure like above.

```{r}
k2 <- kmeans(z, centers=4)
plot(z, col=k2$cluster)
points(k2$centers, col=7, pch=16, cex=1.5)
```


#### Q. Run `kmeans()` with different values of `centers` between 1 and 10.

```{r}
ans <- NULL
#null just means the variable exists but theres nothing in it

for(i in 1:10) {
  #cat(i, "\n")
  k <- kmeans(z, centers = i)
  ans <- c(ans, k$tot.withinss)
}
```

```{r}
ans
plot(ans, type="o")
```

## Hierarchical Clustering

The main function for heirarchical clustering in base R is called `hclust()`.

This function does not take our "raw" data directly, rather you must provide it with a "distance matrix" computed from your data. 

```{r}
d <- dist(z)
hc <- hclust(d)
hc
```

There is a specific plot method for hc results:
```{r}
plot(hc)
abline(h=8, col="red")
```

We can "cut" our tree at a given height to yield groupings (i.e. clusters). In r we do this with `cutree()`
```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```

We can also run `cutree()` with `k=2` instead of a give `h=` height value.

```{r}
grps <- cutree(hc, k=2)
grps
```


#### Make a results figure of our data `z` colored by our Hierarchical Clustering results.

```{r}
plot(z, col=grps)
```


## Principal Component Analysis

Here we play with some silly data on the unhealthy eating habits of ppl from the UK.

### Data import

>This is copied from the lab on the coursewebsite, but edited with the `row.names=1` bit

```{r}
url <- "https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods"
x <- read.csv(url, row.names = 1)
x
```


```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

A plot that is useful is the pairs plot (for pairwise comparisons):

```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```

```{r}
library(pheatmap)
pheatmap( as.matrix(x) )
```

>These are all kinda booty, finding relationships in out data is hard and be need something better.

## PCA to the rescue

The main function in base r is called `prcomp()`.

For this function we will want to take the transpose of our data so we analyze the foods. 

```{r}
# t(x) makes the foods the columns instead of the countries
pca <- prcomp(t(x))
```

We can see how well our pca PCs are doing:

```{r}
summary(pca)
```
>bc the proportion of variance is like almost 100% within the first 2 PCs means that nearly all the variance in this dataset can be captured on only two axes. 

Lets graph it, so lets call ggplot bc we miss ggplot so much.
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
```

Our main PC plot results figure:

```{r}
ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(PC1, PC2) +
  geom_point(col=c("orange", "red", "blue", "darkgreen"))
```

The final plot is called a loadings plot: how the original variables contribute to the PC1.

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1, row.names(pca$rotation)) +
  geom_col()
```
